title: Long EWJ — Japan Oil Import Relief + AI Memory Demand Recovery (MU HBM4 Readthrough)
entry: Long $92-96 (EWJ at ~$94 on June 25; Nikkei 225 closed +4.61% on June 25 as Japan recovers from Iran-conflict energy shock). Scale: 60% initial in the $92-95 range on June 25 or the morning of June 26; 40% add on any pullback to $91-93 on the June 26 Russell reconstitution volatility spill-over if the rebalancing creates a temporary dip in Asia-linked ETFs. Do NOT enter above $97 — at that level the Nikkei single-day recovery is fully priced.
stop_loss: $89 daily close (~4.3% below $93 midpoint) — implies Brent oil reverses back above $80-82 on Hormuz implementation delay, erasing the energy import relief thesis for Japan, OR the yen strengthens materially (below 145 USD/JPY) on a risk-off event that simultaneously hurts Japanese export earnings, OR MU's HBM4 revenue confirmation proves to not translate to DRAM/HBM demand from Japanese supply chain names (Renesas, TDK, Murata)
targets: $98 — Nikkei consolidates above the +4% recovery; Japan electronics names (TDK, Murata, Kyocera) begin benefiting from MU HBM4 supply chain readthrough; EWJ approaches pre-Iran-conflict May 2026 levels; +5.4% from $93 midpoint

$103 — BoJ June meeting (June 26-27): if BoJ confirms no rate hike and maintains yield curve control upper bound, the yen/export earnings combination sustains the Nikkei rally; sell-side upgrades Japan equity market on dual energy + tech demand tailwinds; +10.8%

$110 — structural re-rating: Japan confirmed as AI semiconductor supply chain beneficiary; TSMC-Japan (JASM) Kumamoto fab announcement adds further demand confidence; EWJ re-rates to late 2024 highs; +18.3%
catalyst: Two converging catalysts materialized for Japan equities on June 25: (1) Brent crude at $73.05 (down 5.2% from June 24) following the Hormuz reopening — Japan imports ~87% of its oil and LNG, making it the single largest per-capita beneficiary of oil normalization after the Iran conflict; cheaper energy directly improves Japan's trade balance and reduces the BoJ's inflation pressure from imported goods. (2) MU's Q3 FY2026 earnings ($41.5B revenue vs. $34.66B consensus, +20% beat) on AI-driven HBM4 memory demand reads through directly to Japan's semiconductor supply chain: Renesas (MCUs), TDK and Murata (capacitors for HBM substrates), and Kyocera (semiconductor packaging) are all EWJ-constituent companies with direct exposure to memory-adjacent demand. The Nikkei 225 surged +4.61% on June 25, catching up from Japan's June 24 holiday. The Nikkei is still below its conflict-period ATH near 42,500 — the recovery has room to run.
thesis:
Japan's equity market is the most structurally levered major economy to two of the three dominant macro themes of June 25: oil normalization and AI semiconductor demand. EWJ (iShares MSCI Japan ETF) captures these themes across a diversified basket of ~240 Japanese equities, reducing single-stock risk while maintaining broad exposure to the recovery dynamics.

On oil: Japan spends approximately 18-22 trillion yen annually on energy imports. At the Iran-conflict peak (Brent $90-93), Japan's monthly energy import bill was running $15-17B/month above pre-conflict baseline — a direct drag on corporate margins for every energy-intensive Japanese manufacturer (steel, chemicals, automotive, shipping). At Brent $73, the monthly savings versus conflict-peak run to $8-10B — a direct margin tailwind that does not require a demand catalyst; it is mechanical from lower input costs. Toyota, Honda, Nippon Steel, and Mitsubishi Chemical are all top EWJ holdings and all have material energy cost exposure.

On AI semiconductors: Japan's downstream component suppliers (TDK, Murata, Kyocera, Renesas) supply critical materials into the HBM memory substrate and packaging supply chain. MU's $41.5B Q3 revenue confirms that AI memory demand is not a forecast but a current reality. The MU Q4 guide of $50B ± $1B implies the demand acceleration is continuing — and that supply chain demand flows to Japan's component makers within one to two quarters with a well-documented lag. The Nikkei's +4.61% move on June 25 partially reflects this readthrough; the complete repricing across supply chain names takes 2-4 weeks as sell-side Japan equity analysts update models.

The risk is currency: EWJ returns are USD-denominated, and the yen has been weak (~152-155 USD/JPY) on the BofA 3-hike narrative. A stronger yen (from BoJ normalization or risk-off) would reduce USD returns from the Nikkei rally. The BoJ meeting on June 26-27 is the primary near-term risk — if BoJ signals a rate hike to defend yen purchasing power on import inflation, the yen could strengthen sharply, and the EWJ position (unhedged) could see currency gains offset equity rally partially. This is why the position is sized at 2% and the conviction is low — the thesis is sound but the currency overlay creates execution risk that requires monitoring.
bull_case: BoJ June 26-27 meeting maintains no-hike stance; yen holds at 152-155. Nikkei consolidates gains and extends toward 41,500 over 10 sessions. Sell-side upgrades Japan equity: Morgan Stanley and Goldman upgrade OVERWEIGHT on Japan on dual oil relief + AI supply chain tailwind. EWJ reaches $98 (Target 1) within 10 days and $103 (Target 2) by mid-July as the MU supply chain readthrough flows into Q2 Japan earnings guidance.
bear_case: BoJ June 26-27 surprises with a 25bp rate hike (yen strengthens to 148-150). Simultaneously, Brent crude partially recovers to $78-80 on OPEC+ emergency production cut concerns. The dual headwind of yen appreciation (hurts exporters) and fading energy relief compresses the Nikkei back toward 38,500. EWJ falls from $94 toward $90-91, approaching the $89 stop on a BoJ surprise scenario.
invalidation: $89 daily EWJ close; OR BoJ announces rate hike at June 26-27 meeting above 0.25% (yen appreciation eliminates unhedged USD returns); OR Brent crude closes above $80 for two consecutive sessions (Hormuz implementation collapse or OPEC+ emergency cut reverses energy relief); OR USD/JPY breaks below 148 on a sustained basis (yen appreciation structurally reduces USD EWJ returns)
